title: The Case of the Wet Book
story: A library book came back with wet pages. Mrs. Kim looked for clues. The book was in Sam's blue bag. Sam's water bottle was in the same bag. The lid was not screwed on all the way. Ava had the book last week. She gave it back dry. The wet spot starts where the bottle sat.
question: What made the book wet?

suspects.why: in the same bag, with the lid not screwed on
she gave it back dry
the wet spot starts where the bottle sat

answer: Sam's water bottle leaked on the book.
proof: “Sam's water bottle was in the same bag.”
“The lid was not screwed on all the way.”
clears: Ava: “She gave it back dry.”
Rain: “The wet spot starts where the bottle sat.”
explain: The wet spot starts where the bottle sat. Because the lid was not screwed on all the way, the water leaked onto the book.

debate.story: A library book came back with wet pages. The book was in Sam's blue bag. Sam's water bottle was in the same bag. The lid was not screwed on. Ava had the book last week. It rained hard on the day she walked home. Sam's bag has a hole in the bottom. The wet spot is on the back cover.
debate.question: What made the book wet? Say who, and read out the words.

suspects.why: a bottle in the same bag with the lid not screwed on
had the book last week, when it rained hard
hard rain, and a bag with a hole in the bottom

evidence: “Sam's water bottle was in the same bag.”
“The lid was not screwed on.”
arguments.against: “It rained hard on the day she walked home.”

evidence: “Ava had the book last week.”
arguments.against: “The wet spot is on the back cover.”

evidence: “It rained hard on the day she walked home.”
“Sam's bag has a hole in the bottom.”
arguments.against: “Sam's water bottle was in the same bag.”

debate.note: Ask where the wet spot is and what sits there. A bottle lying on its side wets the middle; rain through a hole in the bottom wets the back cover. The children do not need the word evidence to do this. They need to point.

title: The Case of the Empty Snack Bag
story: Mia packed apple slices in a snack bag. At lunch the bag was empty. The bag had a small hole in one corner. A line of apple slices lay in her backpack. Her friend Jo ate her own lunch. Mia had not opened the bag yet. The slices were still cold. Nobody else touched her bag.
question: Where did the apple slices go?

suspects.why: a line of slices lay in her backpack
Jo ate her own lunch
Mia had not opened the bag yet

answer: The slices fell out through the hole.
proof: “The bag had a small hole in one corner.”
“A line of apple slices lay in her backpack.”
clears: Jo: “Her friend Jo ate her own lunch.”
Mia: “Mia had not opened the bag yet.”
explain: A line of slices lay in her backpack. Because the bag had a hole in one corner, the slices fell out one at a time.

debate.story: Mia packed apple slices in a snack bag. At lunch the bag was empty. The bag had a small hole in one corner. A line of slices lay in her backpack. Jo sat next to Mia on the bus. Mia had a sticky hand at nine o'clock. The slices in the bag were still cold.
debate.question: Where did the apple slices go? Pick one and show the words.

suspects.why: a hole in one corner, with a line of slices in the pack
sat next to Mia on the bus
a sticky hand at nine o'clock

evidence: “The bag had a small hole in one corner.”
“A line of slices lay in her backpack.”
arguments.against: “Mia had a sticky hand at nine o'clock.”

evidence: “Jo sat next to Mia on the bus.”
arguments.against: “A line of slices lay in her backpack.”

evidence: “Mia had a sticky hand at nine o'clock.”
arguments.against: “The bag had a small hole in one corner.”

debate.note: A line of slices is the picture to draw on the board. Things that fall make a line; things that are eaten do not. Sitting next to somebody is not evidence of anything, and saying so is a fine answer for a seven-year-old.

title: The Case of the Short Pencil
story: Ben's new pencil was long on Monday. On Friday it was very short. Ben did not lose it. Nobody else used it. The sharpener was full of his shavings. Ben likes to make the tip sharp. He sharpened it after every page. The pencil is still his pencil. It just got smaller.
question: Why is the pencil so short?

suspects.why: the sharpener was full of his shavings
Ben did not lose it
nobody else used it

answer: Ben sharpened the pencil down.
proof: “The sharpener was full of his shavings.”
“He sharpened it after every page.”
clears: Losing it: “Ben did not lose it.”
Somebody taking it: “Nobody else used it.”
explain: The pencil is still his pencil. Because he sharpened it after every page, the shavings filled the sharpener and the pencil got shorter.

debate.story: Ben's new pencil was long on Monday. On Friday it was very short. The sharpener was full of his shavings. Ben sharpens after every page. Ben left his pencil on the rug on Wednesday. Two pencils in the cup look just like his. Ben's name is not on any of them.
debate.question: Why is Ben's pencil short? Choose one and read out the words.

suspects.why: a sharpener full of his shavings, after every page
left on the rug on Wednesday
two in the cup that look just like his, with no name

evidence: “The sharpener was full of his shavings.”
“Ben sharpens after every page.”
arguments.against: “Ben left his pencil on the rug on Wednesday.”

evidence: “Ben left his pencil on the rug on Wednesday.”
arguments.against: “The sharpener was full of his shavings.”

evidence: “Two pencils in the cup look just like his.”
“Ben's name is not on any of them.”
arguments.against: “Ben sharpens after every page.”

debate.note: If the pencil is short, it is still his pencil and it got smaller. If it was swapped, the short one belongs to somebody else. Ask the class which story the shavings fit, and then ask how Ben could ever tell his pencil from the others.

title: The Case of the Soft Apples
story: Room 5 picked apples on Monday. By Friday six were soft and brown. The six soft ones sat in a sunny spot. The rest sat in the cool hall. Nobody dropped the apples. All the apples came from one tree. The soft ones smell sweet. Warm air makes an apple go soft fast.
question: Why did six apples go soft?

suspects.why: the six soft ones sat in a sunny spot
all the apples came from one tree
nobody dropped the apples

answer: The warm sunny spot made the apples soft.
proof: “The six soft ones sat in a sunny spot.”
“Warm air makes an apple go soft fast.”
clears: A bad tree: “All the apples came from one tree.”
Dropping: “Nobody dropped the apples.”
explain: The apples in the cool hall are still firm. Because the six soft ones sat in a sunny spot, the warm air made them go soft.

debate.story: Room 5 picked apples on Monday. By Friday six were soft and brown. The six soft ones sat in a sunny spot. The rest sat in the cool hall. The six came off the low branch by the road. The crate was dropped once on the way in. Warm air makes an apple go soft fast.
debate.question: Why did six apples go soft? Say which one, and show the words.

suspects.why: a sunny spot, where warm air makes an apple soft fast
all six off the low branch by the road
a crate dropped once on the way in

evidence: “The six soft ones sat in a sunny spot.”
“Warm air makes an apple go soft fast.”
arguments.against: “The six came off the low branch by the road.”

evidence: “The six came off the low branch by the road.”
arguments.against: “The rest sat in the cool hall.”

evidence: “The crate was dropped once on the way in.”
arguments.against: “The six soft ones sat in a sunny spot.”

debate.note: The same six apples came off one branch and sat in one sunny spot, so the case has two answers pointing at the same fruit. That is worth saying plainly. Children who notice the six are the same six, twice over, have found the hard part.

title: The Case of the Squeaky Bike
story: Lin's bike squeaked on every ride. The squeak came from the back wheel. Her dad looked at the chain. The chain was dry and dusty. The tires were full of air. The brakes were tight and clean. Nothing was bent or broken. He put oil on the chain. The squeak stopped.
question: What made the bike squeak?

suspects.why: the chain was dry and dusty
the tires were full of air
the brakes were tight and clean

answer: The dry chain made the squeak.
proof: “The chain was dry and dusty.”
“He put oil on the chain.”
clears: The tires: “The tires were full of air.”
The brakes: “The brakes were tight and clean.”
explain: The squeak stopped after the oil went on. Because the chain was dry and dusty, it squeaked on every ride.

debate.story: Lin's bike squeaked on every ride. The squeak came from the back wheel. The chain was dry and dusty. The back tire was soft and rubbed the frame. The back brake pad touched the wheel all the time. Her dad put oil on the chain. The squeak got quieter but did not stop.
debate.question: What is squeaking? Pick one and read out the words.

suspects.why: a chain that was dry and dusty
a soft back tire that rubbed the frame
a back pad touching the wheel all the time

evidence: “The chain was dry and dusty.”
“Her dad put oil on the chain.”
arguments.against: “The squeak got quieter but did not stop.”

evidence: “The back tire was soft and rubbed the frame.”
arguments.against: “The chain was dry and dusty.”

evidence: “The back brake pad touched the wheel all the time.”
arguments.against: “Her dad put oil on the chain.”

debate.note: Quieter but not stopped is the whole case in four words. Something was fixed and something is left. Ask the class what that tells them, and look for the child who says there must be two squeaks.

title: The Case of the Green Water
story: The fish tank water turned green. The class checked the filter twice. The filter was clean and running. Both tanks got the same food. The tank sits in front of a sunny window. Green plants grow fast in sunlight. A second tank sits in the dark hall. That water is still clear.
question: Why did the water turn green?

suspects.why: the tank in the dark hall is still clear
the filter was clean and running
both tanks got the same food

answer: Sunlight made tiny green plants grow.
proof: “The tank sits in front of a sunny window.”
“Green plants grow fast in sunlight.”
clears: The filter: “The filter was clean and running.”
Food: “Both tanks got the same food.”
explain: The tank in the dark hall is still clear. Because this tank sits in a sunny window, green plants grew fast in the light.

debate.story: The fish tank water turned green. The tank sits in front of a sunny window. Green plants grow fast in sunlight. The filter has not been washed since the fall. Two helpers both fed the fish on Friday. A second tank sits in the dark hall. That water is still clear.
debate.question: Why did the water turn green? Choose one and show the words.

suspects.why: a sunny window, where green plants grow fast
a filter not washed since the fall
two helpers who both fed the fish on Friday

evidence: “The tank sits in front of a sunny window.”
“A second tank sits in the dark hall.”
arguments.against: “The filter has not been washed since the fall.”

evidence: “The filter has not been washed since the fall.”
arguments.against: “That water is still clear.”

evidence: “Two helpers both fed the fish on Friday.”
arguments.against: “Green plants grow fast in sunlight.”

debate.note: The dark hall tank is the one to keep coming back to. Same room, same food, no sun, clear water. Children who use it are comparing two things on purpose, which is the beginning of every experiment they will ever run.

title: The Case of the Buzzing Light
story: A buzz came from the ceiling in Room 2. It buzzed only in the morning. The class turns the lights on at eight. One long light bulb flickers when it buzzes. The clock on the wall is quiet. No bees were in the room. Mr. Lee changed that bulb. The buzzing went away.
question: What was buzzing?

suspects.why: one long bulb flickers when it buzzes
the clock on the wall is quiet
no bees were in the room

answer: A bad light bulb made the buzz.
proof: “One long light bulb flickers when it buzzes.”
“Mr. Lee changed that bulb.”
clears: The clock: “The clock on the wall is quiet.”
A bee: “No bees were in the room.”
explain: The buzzing went away after the bulb was changed. Because the bulb flickers when it buzzes, that bulb was making the sound.

debate.story: A buzz came from the ceiling in Room 2. It buzzed only in the morning. One long light bulb flickers when it buzzes. The class turns the lights on at eight. The clock buzzes too when its battery is low. A bee nest sits under the roof outside that wall. Bees are busy in the morning sun.
debate.question: What is buzzing? Pick one and read out the words.

suspects.why: a long bulb that flickers when it buzzes
a clock that buzzes when its battery is low
a nest under the roof, and bees busy in the morning

evidence: “One long light bulb flickers when it buzzes.”
“The class turns the lights on at eight.”
arguments.against: “A bee nest sits under the roof outside that wall.”

evidence: “The clock buzzes too when its battery is low.”
arguments.against: “One long light bulb flickers when it buzzes.”

evidence: “A bee nest sits under the roof outside that wall.”
“Bees are busy in the morning sun.”
arguments.against: “The class turns the lights on at eight.”

debate.note: Two things happen in the morning here: the lights go on and the bees wake up. Only in the morning used to point at one answer and now it points at two. The flickering bulb is the only clue you can see as well as hear.

title: The Case of the Moving Leaves
story: Room 3 raked leaves into one big pile. The pile was neat on Monday. The next day the leaves were spread out. No footprints were in the pile. The gate was shut all night. A strong wind blew all night long. The leaves lie in a long line. The line points away from the wind.
question: What spread the leaves out?

suspects.why: the leaves lie in a long line
no footprints were in the pile
the gate was shut all night

answer: The wind blew the leaves into a line.
proof: “A strong wind blew all night long.”
“The leaves lie in a long line.”
clears: Somebody walking: “No footprints were in the pile.”
A dog: “The gate was shut all night.”
explain: The line points away from the wind. Because a strong wind blew all night, it spread the pile into a long line.

debate.story: Room 3 raked leaves into one big pile. The next day the leaves were spread out. A strong wind blew all night long. The leaves lie in a long line. Two small footprints sit at the edge of the pile. The gate was open on Tuesday night. Dog hair is caught in the leaves.
debate.question: What spread the leaves? Say which one, and show the words.

suspects.why: a strong wind all night, and leaves in a long line
two small footprints at the edge of the pile
an open gate, and dog hair caught in the leaves

evidence: “A strong wind blew all night long.”
“The leaves lie in a long line.”
arguments.against: “Two small footprints sit at the edge of the pile.”

evidence: “Two small footprints sit at the edge of the pile.”
arguments.against: “A strong wind blew all night long.”

evidence: “The gate was open on Tuesday night.”
“Dog hair is caught in the leaves.”
arguments.against: “The leaves lie in a long line.”

debate.note: A long line is a shape, and shapes are evidence. Ask what shape a dog would leave and what shape a child jumping in would leave. Two footprints at the edge mean somebody stood there, which is not the same as somebody spreading leaves.

title: The Case of the Leaking Pumpkin
story: The class pumpkin sat by the door. On Monday a puddle was under it. The bottom of the pumpkin was soft. Nobody cut the pumpkin open. No animal came in the room. The pumpkin is ten days old. A soft spot lets the juice out. The puddle is right under the soft spot.
question: Where did the puddle come from?

suspects.who: 🎃 A soft spot on the pumpkin
suspects.why: the puddle is right under the soft spot
nobody cut the pumpkin open
no animal came in the room

answer: The soft spot let juice out of the pumpkin.
proof: “The bottom of the pumpkin was soft.”
“A soft spot lets the juice out.”
clears: Cutting: “Nobody cut the pumpkin open.”
An animal: “No animal came in the room.”
explain: The puddle is right under the soft spot. Because the bottom went soft, the juice leaked out of the pumpkin.

debate.story: The class pumpkin sat by the door. On Monday a puddle was under it. The bottom of the pumpkin was soft. The puddle is right under the soft spot. A thin cut runs across the lid where it was lifted. Small teeth marks show near the stem. The pumpkin is ten days old.
debate.question: Why is there a puddle? Pick one and read out the words.

suspects.who: 🎃 A soft spot on the pumpkin
suspects.why: a soft bottom, with the puddle right under it
a thin cut across the lid where it was lifted
small teeth marks near the stem

evidence: “The bottom of the pumpkin was soft.”
“The puddle is right under the soft spot.”
arguments.against: “A thin cut runs across the lid where it was lifted.”

evidence: “A thin cut runs across the lid where it was lifted.”
arguments.against: “The puddle is right under the soft spot.”

evidence: “Small teeth marks show near the stem.”
arguments.against: “The bottom of the pumpkin was soft.”

debate.note: Right under is the phrase that does the work. Water comes out at the bottom and runs down, so the puddle sits where the hole is. The cut and the teeth marks are both near the top, and children can be asked what that means for a puddle on the floor.

title: The Case of the White Footprints
story: White footprints went down the hall. They came from the art room. The art class used white paint today. The prints are small like a child's shoe. Mr. Ruiz wears big boots. The paint tray sat on the floor. One student stepped in the tray. The prints lead to the sink.
question: Who made the white footprints?

suspects.who: 🎨 A student in the art class
suspects.why: the prints are small and the tray sat on the floor
Mr. Ruiz wears big boots
the prints look like a child's shoe

answer: A student stepped in the paint tray.
proof: “The paint tray sat on the floor.”
“One student stepped in the tray.”
clears: Mr. Ruiz: “Mr. Ruiz wears big boots.”
A dog: “The prints are small like a child's shoe.”
explain: The prints lead to the sink. Because the paint tray sat on the floor, one student stepped in it and walked away.

debate.story: White footprints went down the hall. They came from the art room. The art class used white paint today. Each print is the size of a child's shoe. The paint tray sat on the floor. Mr. Ruiz keeps white shoes for the gym. A dog came in with the office helper at ten.
debate.question: Who left the white prints? Choose one and show the words.

suspects.who: 🎨 A student in the art class
suspects.why: small prints from the art room, with the tray on the floor
keeps white shoes for the gym
came in with the office helper at ten

evidence: “The art class used white paint today.”
“The paint tray sat on the floor.”
arguments.against: “Mr. Ruiz keeps white shoes for the gym.”

evidence: “Mr. Ruiz keeps white shoes for the gym.”
arguments.against: “Each print is the size of a child's shoe.”

evidence: “A dog came in with the office helper at ten.”
arguments.against: “They came from the art room.”

debate.note: White shoes and white paint are two different whites, and that is a lovely thing for a class to untangle. A shoe print and a paw print look different too. Ask what the prints would look like for each suspect before anybody chooses.

title: The Case of the Left Coat
story: Theo could not find his red coat. He wore it on the bus. He took it off because the bus was warm. The driver found a red coat on seat 4. Theo always sits in seat 4. His mom looked all over the house. He checked his cubby too. The coat was not there.
question: Where was the coat?

suspects.why: the driver found a red coat on seat 4
his mom looked all over the house
he took it off on the bus

answer: The coat was on the bus in seat 4.
proof: “The driver found a red coat on seat 4.”
“Theo always sits in seat 4.”
clears: At home: “His mom looked all over the house.”
At school: “He took it off because the bus was warm.”
explain: Theo always sits in seat 4. Because he took his coat off on the warm bus, it stayed on his seat.

debate.story: Theo could not find his red coat. He wore it on the bus. The driver found a red coat on seat 4. Theo always sits in seat 4. Two boys in his class have red coats. His mom has not looked in the car yet. He hung a coat in his cubby at nine.
debate.question: Where is the coat? Pick one and read out the words.

suspects.why: a red coat on seat 4, where he always sits
a car that nobody has looked in yet
a coat hung in his cubby at nine

evidence: “The driver found a red coat on seat 4.”
“Theo always sits in seat 4.”
arguments.against: “Two boys in his class have red coats.”

evidence: “His mom has not looked in the car yet.”
arguments.against: “He wore it on the bus.”

evidence: “He hung a coat in his cubby at nine.”
arguments.against: “The driver found a red coat on seat 4.”

debate.note: Two boys with red coats is the sentence that makes this hard. A red coat on seat 4 is a red coat. Ask the children how Theo could be sure it is his, and somebody will say to look inside it for his name.

title: The Case of the Dusty Trophy
story: The reading trophy looked shiny in the fall. Now it looks gray. The case has no door on the back. The shelf is next to an open window. Gray dust sits on the window sill. No one has touched the trophy. Mrs. Diaz wiped it with a cloth. It was shiny again.
question: Why did the trophy look gray?

suspects.why: gray dust sits on the window sill
no one has touched the trophy
a wipe made it shiny again

answer: Dust from the open window made it gray.
proof: “The shelf is next to an open window.”
“Gray dust sits on the window sill.”
clears: Handling: “No one has touched the trophy.”
Paint: “It was shiny again.”
explain: A wipe made the trophy shiny again. Because the case has no back and sits by an open window, gray dust settled on it.

debate.story: The reading trophy looked shiny in the fall. Now it looks gray. The shelf is next to an open window. Gray dust sits on the window sill. The trophy was passed around the class in November. Its gold coat is worn thin at the handles. A wipe with a cloth made it shiny again.
debate.question: Why does the trophy look gray? Say which one, and show the words.

suspects.why: gray dust on the sill beside an open window
passed around the whole class in November
a gold coat worn thin at the handles

evidence: “Gray dust sits on the window sill.”
“The shelf is next to an open window.”
arguments.against: “The trophy was passed around the class in November.”

evidence: “The trophy was passed around the class in November.”
arguments.against: “A wipe with a cloth made it shiny again.”

evidence: “Its gold coat is worn thin at the handles.”
arguments.against: “A wipe with a cloth made it shiny again.”

debate.note: A wipe fixed it, and that one fact decides a lot. Dust comes off on a cloth. Worn paint does not come back. Ask the class what a cloth can and cannot do, and the answer sorts itself out.

title: The Case of the Cold Rolls
story: The class made rolls for the fall feast. The rolls came out cold in the middle. The oven was on at the right heat. The rolls baked for the right time. Ten rolls were stacked in one pan. Rolls in the middle of a stack stay cold. The rolls on the edge were warm.
question: Why were the rolls cold inside?

suspects.why: rolls in the middle of a stack stay cold
the oven was on at the right heat
the rolls baked for the right time

answer: The rolls were stacked too close together.
proof: “Ten rolls were stacked in one pan.”
“Rolls in the middle of a stack stay cold.”
clears: The oven: “The oven was on at the right heat.”
Time: “The rolls baked for the right time.”
explain: The rolls on the edge were warm. Because ten rolls were stacked in one pan, the heat could not reach the middle ones.

debate.story: The class made rolls for the fall feast. The rolls came out cold in the middle. Ten rolls were stacked in one pan. The rolls on the edge were warm. The oven door does not shut all the way. The timer rang before anyone set it twice. Rolls in the middle of a stack stay cold.
debate.question: Why were the rolls cold inside? Choose one and read out the words.

suspects.why: ten in one pan, where the middle of a stack stays cold
a door that does not shut all the way
a timer that rang before anyone set it twice

evidence: “Ten rolls were stacked in one pan.”
“Rolls in the middle of a stack stay cold.”
arguments.against: “The oven door does not shut all the way.”

evidence: “The oven door does not shut all the way.”
arguments.against: “The rolls on the edge were warm.”

evidence: “The timer rang before anyone set it twice.”
arguments.against: “The rolls on the edge were warm.”

debate.note: The rolls on the edge were warm, and that sentence beats two of the three answers on its own. A cold oven or a short time makes every roll cold. Only the stack makes the middle ones cold and the edge ones warm.

title: The Case of the Sunken Cupcakes
story: Room 1 baked cupcakes for a party. Each cupcake looked fine at first. Each one sank in the middle. The class opened the oven to look. They opened it three times. Cool air makes a cake fall. The batter was mixed just right. The oven was the right heat. The edges rose fine.
question: Why did the cupcakes sink?

suspects.why: they opened it three times
the batter was mixed just right
the oven was the right heat

answer: Cool air from the open oven made them fall.
proof: “They opened it three times.”
“Cool air makes a cake fall.”
clears: The batter: “The batter was mixed just right.”
The oven: “The oven was the right heat.”
explain: The edges rose fine. Because the class opened the oven three times, cool air got in and the middles sank.

debate.story: Room 1 baked cupcakes for a party. Each one sank in the middle. The class opened the oven three times to look. Cool air makes a cake fall. The batter was stirred for ten minutes. The oven dial sits between two numbers. Nobody wrote the heat down. The edges rose fine.
debate.question: Why did the cupcakes sink? Pick one and show the words.

suspects.why: a door opened three times, and cool air makes a cake fall
batter stirred for ten minutes
a dial sitting between two numbers, with nothing written down

evidence: “The class opened the oven three times to look.”
“Cool air makes a cake fall.”
arguments.against: “The batter was stirred for ten minutes.”

evidence: “The batter was stirred for ten minutes.”
arguments.against: “The edges rose fine.”

evidence: “The oven dial sits between two numbers.”
“Nobody wrote the heat down.”
arguments.against: “The edges rose fine.”

debate.note: The edges rose and the middles sank, which means the cakes started well and stopped. Ask when each suspect would have gone wrong. Bad batter would never rise at all, and a door opened three times goes wrong in the middle of the bake.

title: The Case of the One Wet Glove
story: Ana has two gloves. One glove is wet and one is dry. She made a snowball with her right hand. Her right glove is the wet one. She kept her left hand in her pocket. Both gloves hung by the heater all night. Snow melts into a glove that touches it.
question: Why is one glove wet?

suspects.why: she made it with her right hand
both gloves hung by the heater
she kept her left hand in her pocket

answer: The snowball made her right glove wet.
proof: “She made a snowball with her right hand.”
“Her right glove is the wet one.”
clears: The heater: “Both gloves hung by the heater all night.”
Her other hand: “She kept her left hand in her pocket.”
explain: Both gloves hung by the same heater. Because she made a snowball with her right hand, snow melted into only that glove.

debate.story: Ana has two gloves. One glove is wet and one is dry. She made a snowball with her right hand. Her right glove is the wet one. Her right glove also hung closest to the heater. A hot heater makes snow on a glove melt fast. She walked home in the rain with one hand out.
debate.question: Why is one glove wet? Pick one and read out the words.

suspects.why: made with her right hand, and the right glove is wet
the right glove hung closest to the heater
walked home in the rain with one hand out

evidence: “She made a snowball with her right hand.”
“Her right glove is the wet one.”
arguments.against: “Her right glove also hung closest to the heater.”

evidence: “Her right glove also hung closest to the heater.”
“A hot heater makes snow on a glove melt fast.”
arguments.against: “One glove is wet and one is dry.”

evidence: “She walked home in the rain with one hand out.”
arguments.against: “She made a snowball with her right hand.”

debate.note: Three things happened to the right hand and nothing happened to the left. Say that out loud and let the class see the shape of it. The heater answer is the sly one, because it does not wet a glove so much as melt what was already on it.

title: The Case of the Sliding Candy
story: Room 6 stuck candy on a gingerbread house. By morning the candy slid down. The class used soft frosting for glue. Soft frosting never gets hard. The candy on the roof fell first. No one bumped the house. The walls of the house still stand. Another class used hard icing. Their candy stayed on.
question: Why did the candy slide off?

suspects.why: soft frosting never gets hard
no one bumped the house
the other class's candy stayed on

answer: The soft frosting never got hard.
proof: “The class used soft frosting for glue.”
“Soft frosting never gets hard.”
clears: Bumping: “No one bumped the house.”
Heavy candy: “Their candy stayed on.”
explain: Another class used hard icing and their candy stayed on. Because this class used soft frosting, the candy slid down.

debate.story: Room 6 stuck candy on a gingerbread house. By morning the candy slid down. The class used soft frosting for glue. Soft frosting never gets hard. The candy on the roof fell first. The room was warm all night with the heat on. The roof candy is the biggest in the box.
debate.question: Why did the candy slide? Choose one and show the words.

suspects.why: soft frosting for glue, which never gets hard
a warm room all night with the heat on
the roof candy is the biggest in the box

evidence: “The class used soft frosting for glue.”
“Soft frosting never gets hard.”
arguments.against: “The room was warm all night with the heat on.”

evidence: “The room was warm all night with the heat on.”
arguments.against: “Soft frosting never gets hard.”

evidence: “The roof candy is the biggest in the box.”
“The candy on the roof fell first.”
arguments.against: “The class used soft frosting for glue.”

debate.note: The roof candy fell first and it is also the heaviest, which is a clue doing two jobs. Ask why the roof is the hardest place for glue to hold anything. Soft frosting and a warm room are close cousins and children may well say so.

title: The Case of the Dark Window
story: Six lights hang in the school window. Three of them went dark. The dark three are all on one end. One plug joins that end to the wall. The plug was pulled halfway out. The bright three use a different plug. Mr. Cole pushed the plug in. All six lit up.
question: Why were three lights dark?

suspects.why: the plug was pulled halfway out
all six lit up when the plug went in
the bright three use a different plug

answer: A loose plug left that end with no power.
proof: “One plug joins that end to the wall.”
“The plug was pulled halfway out.”
clears: Bulbs: “All six lit up.”
A power cut: “The bright three use a different plug.”
explain: All six lit up when the plug went back in. Because the plug for that end was halfway out, those three lights had no power.

debate.story: Six lights hang in the school window. Three of them went dark. The dark three are all on one end. One plug joins that end to the wall. The plug was pulled halfway out. The first bulb on that end is black inside. The bright three run from a second plug.
debate.question: Why did three lights go dark? Say which one, and show the words.

suspects.why: a plug pulled halfway out of the wall
the first bulb on that end is black inside
the dark three all on one end, on one plug

evidence: “The plug was pulled halfway out.”
“One plug joins that end to the wall.”
arguments.against: “The first bulb on that end is black inside.”

evidence: “The first bulb on that end is black inside.”
arguments.against: “The plug was pulled halfway out.”

evidence: “The dark three are all on one end.”
“The bright three run from a second plug.”
arguments.against: “The plug was pulled halfway out.”

debate.note: Two broken things sit at the same end of the string. A plug half out and a black bulb would each turn off exactly those three lights. Ask the class how they would find out which one, and push the plug in is a very good answer.

title: The Case of the Loud Clock
story: The class clock used to be quiet. Now it ticks very loudly. The clock still shows the right time. Nothing is cracked or bent. The class moved the clock to a bare wall. A bare wall sends sound back into the room. The old wall had a soft bulletin board on it.
question: Why does the clock sound loud now?

suspects.why: a bare wall sends sound back into the room
the clock still shows the right time
nothing is cracked or bent

answer: The bare wall sends the tick back into the room.
proof: “The class moved the clock to a bare wall.”
“A bare wall sends sound back into the room.”
clears: A broken clock: “The clock still shows the right time.”
Damage: “Nothing is cracked or bent.”
explain: The old wall had a soft bulletin board on it. Because the clock now hangs on a bare wall, the tick bounces back into the room.

debate.story: The class clock used to be quiet. Now it ticks very loudly. The class moved the clock to a bare wall. A bare wall sends sound back into the room. The old wall had a soft bulletin board on it. The clock got a new battery the same week. A fresh battery makes the hands push harder.
debate.question: Why is the clock loud now? Pick one and read out the words.

suspects.why: a bare wall that sends sound back into the room
a fresh battery that makes the hands push harder
an old wall with a soft bulletin board on it

evidence: “The class moved the clock to a bare wall.”
“A bare wall sends sound back into the room.”
arguments.against: “The clock got a new battery the same week.”

evidence: “The clock got a new battery the same week.”
“A fresh battery makes the hands push harder.”
arguments.against: “A bare wall sends sound back into the room.”

evidence: “The old wall had a soft bulletin board on it.”
arguments.against: “Now it ticks very loudly.”

debate.note: Two things changed in the same week, which is the oldest trap there is. One is about the clock and two are about the room. Ask what would happen if they put the clock back on the old wall and kept the new battery.

title: The Case of the Short Snowman
story: Room 4 built a snowman on Monday. By Friday it was half as tall. No one knocked it over. The yard was locked all week. Every day was warm and sunny. Water sat in a ring around the snowman. Snow turns to water when the air is warm. The snowman is still standing.
question: Why did the snowman get short?

suspects.why: water sat in a ring around it
no one knocked it over
the yard was locked all week

answer: The warm sun melted the snow into water.
proof: “Every day was warm and sunny.”
“Snow turns to water when the air is warm.”
clears: Knocking: “No one knocked it over.”
An animal: “The yard was locked all week.”
explain: The snowman is still standing and there is water around it. Because every day was warm and sunny, the snow turned to water and the snowman got shorter.

debate.story: Room 4 built a snowman on Monday. By Friday it was half as tall. Every day was warm and sunny. Water sat in a ring around the snowman. Snow turns to water when the air is warm. The gate was found open on Wednesday. Boot prints circle the snowman on one side.
debate.question: Why is the snowman short? Choose one and show the words.

suspects.why: warm sunny days, with water in a ring around it
boot prints circling the snowman on one side
a gate found open on Wednesday

evidence: “Every day was warm and sunny.”
“Water sat in a ring around the snowman.”
arguments.against: “Boot prints circle the snowman on one side.”

evidence: “Boot prints circle the snowman on one side.”
arguments.against: “Snow turns to water when the air is warm.”

evidence: “The gate was found open on Wednesday.”
arguments.against: “Water sat in a ring around the snowman.”

debate.note: A ring of water is the best clue in this story and it is easy to walk past. Where did the water come from, and where did the snow go? Half as tall and still standing is the other one: a push knocks a snowman over, it does not shrink it.

title: The Case of the Tipped Feeder
story: The bird feeder hangs by the window. On Tuesday it hung sideways. One of the two strings was snapped. The snapped end looks chewed, not cut. Squirrel tracks go up the tree. No wind blew that night. The seed spilled under the feeder. Birds are light and small. Birds cannot chew a string.
question: What made the feeder tip?

suspects.why: the end looks chewed and tracks go up the tree
no wind blew that night
birds cannot chew a string

answer: A squirrel chewed through one string.
proof: “The snapped end looks chewed, not cut.”
“Squirrel tracks go up the tree.”
clears: The wind: “No wind blew that night.”
The birds: “Birds cannot chew a string.”
explain: The end looks chewed and tracks go up the tree. Because a squirrel chewed one of the two strings, the feeder hung sideways.

debate.story: The bird feeder hangs by the window. On Tuesday it hung sideways. One of the two strings was snapped. The snapped end looks chewed, not cut. Squirrel tracks go up the tree. The string had been up since last spring. Old string breaks on its own in the cold. Birds use the feeder all day and they are light.
debate.question: What snapped the string? Pick one and read out the words.

suspects.why: a chewed end, with tracks going up the tree
string up since last spring, and old string breaks in the cold
birds are light, and birds cannot chew a string

evidence: “The snapped end looks chewed, not cut.”
“Squirrel tracks go up the tree.”
arguments.against: “The string had been up since last spring.”

evidence: “The string had been up since last spring.”
“Old string breaks on its own in the cold. Birds use the feeder all day and they are light.”
arguments.against: “The snapped end looks chewed, not cut.”

evidence: “On Tuesday it hung sideways.”
arguments.against: “One of the two strings was snapped.”

debate.note: Chewed, not cut is four words that do a lot, and the class should learn to look at an end rather than at a whole. Old string frays when it breaks, which looks different again. Ask what the three kinds of end would look like under a magnifying glass.

title: The Case of the Cool Cocoa
story: The cocoa was hot in the pot. In the cups it was only warm. The cups came out of a cold cupboard. Nobody added cold milk. The pot stayed on the warm stove. A cold cup takes heat from the drink. The class warmed the cups with hot water. The next cocoa stayed hot.
question: Why was the cocoa only warm?

suspects.why: a cold cup takes heat from the drink
nobody added cold milk
the pot stayed on the warm stove

answer: The cold cups took the heat from the cocoa.
proof: “The cups came out of a cold cupboard.”
“A cold cup takes heat from the drink.”
clears: Cold milk: “Nobody added cold milk.”
The pot: “The pot stayed on the warm stove.”
explain: The next cocoa stayed hot after the cups were warmed. Because the cups came from a cold cupboard, they took the heat from the drink.

debate.story: The cocoa was hot in the pot. In the cups it was only warm. The cups came out of a cold cupboard. A cold cup takes heat from the drink. The milk came straight from the fridge. The pot sat off the stove for ten minutes while cups were found.
debate.question: Why was the cocoa only warm? Say which one, and show the words.

suspects.why: cups out of a cold cupboard, taking heat from the drink
milk straight from the fridge
ten minutes off the stove while cups were found

evidence: “The cups came out of a cold cupboard.”
“A cold cup takes heat from the drink.”
arguments.against: “The milk came straight from the fridge.”

evidence: “The milk came straight from the fridge.”
arguments.against: “The cocoa was hot in the pot.”

evidence: “The pot sat off the stove for ten minutes while cups were found.”
arguments.against: “The cups came out of a cold cupboard.”

debate.note: The cocoa was hot in the pot, so whatever cooled it happened after that. Point at the sentence and ask what comes next in the story. Cold milk went in earlier, which puts it out of the running, and children who spot that are reasoning about order.

title: The Case of the Stuck Valentines
story: Room 7 made valentines with red paint. The next day two were stuck together. The two stuck ones were at the bottom of the pile. The ones on top are dry. Wet paint sticks when paper lies on it. The class stacked them right away. The paint was still wet then. Nobody spilled any glue.
question: Why did two valentines stick together?

suspects.why: wet paint sticks when paper lies on it
nobody spilled any glue
the ones on top are dry

answer: Wet paint stuck the bottom two together.
proof: “The class stacked them right away.”
“Wet paint sticks when paper lies on it.”
clears: Glue: “Nobody spilled any glue.”
Water: “The ones on top are dry.”
explain: The two stuck ones were at the bottom of the pile. Because the class stacked them right away, the wet paint stuck the bottom ones together.

debate.story: Room 7 made valentines with red paint. The next day two were stuck together. The two stuck ones were at the bottom of the pile. Wet paint sticks when paper lies on it. The class stacked them right away. Somebody spilled water on the table that afternoon. The glue pot was left open beside the pile.
debate.question: Why are two valentines stuck? Choose one and read out the words.

suspects.why: stacked right away, where wet paint sticks under paper
a glue pot left open beside the pile
water spilled on the table that afternoon

evidence: “The two stuck ones were at the bottom of the pile.”
“Wet paint sticks when paper lies on it.”
arguments.against: “Somebody spilled water on the table that afternoon.”

evidence: “The glue pot was left open beside the pile.”
arguments.against: “The class stacked them right away.”

evidence: “Somebody spilled water on the table that afternoon.”
arguments.against: “Wet paint sticks when paper lies on it.”

debate.note: At the bottom of the pile is the clue that chooses, because that is where the weight is. Water on a table would wet the bottom ones too, so the class has two answers that fit the same two cards. Ask what colour the stuck part is.

title: The Case of the Slow Volcano
story: Sara's model volcano bubbled very slowly at school. It bubbled fast at home. At home she used warm vinegar. At school she used cold vinegar. Cold vinegar bubbles slower than warm. The baking soda came from the same box. The model has no cracks in it. She poured the same amount.
question: Why did the volcano bubble slowly at school?

suspects.why: cold vinegar bubbles slower than warm
it came from the same box
the model has no cracks in it

answer: The cold vinegar bubbled more slowly.
proof: “At school she used cold vinegar.”
“Cold vinegar bubbles slower than warm.”
clears: The baking soda: “The baking soda came from the same box.”
The model: “The model has no cracks in it.”
explain: It bubbled fast at home with warm vinegar. Because she used cold vinegar at school, the bubbling was slow.

debate.story: Sara's model volcano bubbled very slowly at school. It bubbled fast at home. At home she used warm vinegar. At school she used cold vinegar. Cold vinegar bubbles slower than warm. The school box of baking soda had been open all term. The school cone has a much smaller hole at the top.
debate.question: Why was it slow at school? Pick one and show the words.

suspects.why: cold vinegar at school, where cold bubbles slower
a box of baking soda open all term
a cone with a much smaller hole at the top

evidence: “At school she used cold vinegar.”
“Cold vinegar bubbles slower than warm.”
arguments.against: “The school box of baking soda had been open all term.”

evidence: “The school box of baking soda had been open all term.”
arguments.against: “At home she used warm vinegar.”

evidence: “The school cone has a much smaller hole at the top.”
arguments.against: “Cold vinegar bubbles slower than warm.”

debate.note: Three things were different between home and school, and only one of them is about the bubbles themselves. A small hole does not make less foam, it lets less out. Ask the class whether slow means less or just slower, because those are two different stories.

title: The Case of the Loose Crown
story: Kai's paper crown fit at the first play. At the show it slid down. The crown is the same size. Nobody bent it or cut it. Kai got a haircut on Friday. Short hair takes up less room. The crown now needs a clip. His hair is much shorter than before.
question: Why did the crown slide down?

suspects.why: short hair takes up less room
the crown is the same size
nobody bent it or cut it

answer: The haircut left less hair to hold the crown.
proof: “Kai got a haircut on Friday.”
“Short hair takes up less room.”
clears: The crown: “The crown is the same size.”
Bending: “Nobody bent it or cut it.”
explain: The crown is the same size as before. Because Kai got a haircut, there was less hair to hold the crown up.

debate.story: Kai's paper crown fit at the first play. At the show it slid down. Kai got a haircut on Friday. Short hair takes up less room. The crown sat in a damp box over the weekend. Damp paper stretches and goes floppy. Kai wore a hat all morning before the show.
debate.question: Why did the crown slide down? Say which one, and read out the words.

suspects.why: a haircut on Friday, and short hair takes less room
a damp box over the weekend, where paper stretches

suspects.who: 🧢 The hat he wore all morning
suspects.why: a hat worn all morning before the show

evidence: “Kai got a haircut on Friday.”
“Short hair takes up less room.”
arguments.against: “The crown sat in a damp box over the weekend.”

evidence: “The crown sat in a damp box over the weekend.”
“Damp paper stretches and goes floppy.”
arguments.against: “Kai got a haircut on Friday.”

evidence: “Kai wore a hat all morning before the show.”
arguments.against: “Kai's paper crown fit at the first play.”

debate.note: Two things can make a crown too big: a smaller head or a bigger crown. Write those on the board and sort the suspects into them. A class that can name the two ways has understood something, whichever name they end up picking.

title: The Case of the Quiet Key
story: One key on the class piano made no sound. The other keys all work. Mr. Okafor looked inside the piano. A pencil had fallen onto the strings. The pencil sat under that one hammer. A hammer cannot hit a string through a pencil. He took the pencil out. The key worked again.
question: Why did one key make no sound?

suspects.why: the pencil sat under that one hammer
the key worked again once the pencil came out
the other keys all work

answer: A pencil blocked the hammer from the string.
proof: “A pencil had fallen onto the strings.”
“The pencil sat under that one hammer.”
clears: A broken key: “The key worked again.”
The other keys: “The other keys all work.”
explain: The key worked again once the pencil came out. Because the pencil sat under that hammer, the hammer could not reach the string.

debate.story: One key on the class piano made no sound. Every other key makes its sound. Mr. Okafor looked inside the piano. A pencil had fallen onto the strings. The pencil sat under that one hammer. The felt on that hammer is worn away to the wood. A bare hammer makes a thin sound, not none at all.
debate.question: Why is one key silent? Choose one and show the words.

suspects.why: a pencil on the strings, right under that one hammer
felt worn away to the wood on that hammer

suspects.who: 🧐 What a bare hammer sounds like
suspects.why: a bare hammer makes a thin sound, not none at all

evidence: “A pencil had fallen onto the strings.”
“The pencil sat under that one hammer.”
arguments.against: “The felt on that hammer is worn away to the wood.”

evidence: “The felt on that hammer is worn away to the wood.”
arguments.against: “A pencil had fallen onto the strings.”

evidence: “A bare hammer makes a thin sound, not none at all.”
“Every other key makes its sound.”
arguments.against: “The pencil sat under that one hammer.”

debate.note: No sound at all is the thing to hold on to. A worn hammer still makes a sound, so it cannot be the whole answer. Taking the pencil out and listening again is the test, and it costs nothing.

title: The Case of the Low Kite
story: Omar's kite would not go up high. It flew high last Saturday. Today he flew it near the school wall. The wall blocks the wind on that side. Out in the open field the wind is strong. His string is not tangled. He used the same kite both days. The kite has no rips in it.
question: Why would the kite not go high?

suspects.why: the wall blocks the wind on that side
his string is not tangled
the kite has no rips in it

answer: The wall blocked the wind near the school.
proof: “Today he flew it near the school wall.”
“The wall blocks the wind on that side.”
clears: A tangled string: “His string is not tangled.”
A rip: “The kite has no rips in it.”
explain: Out in the open field the wind is strong. Because he flew the kite near the wall, the wall blocked the wind.

debate.story: Omar's kite would not go up high. It flew high last Saturday. Today he flew it near the school wall. The wall blocks the wind on that side. Out in the open field the wind is strong. He added a longer tail this morning. A heavy tail holds a kite down.
debate.question: Why would the kite not go high? Pick one and read out the words.

suspects.why: flown near a wall that blocks the wind on that side
a longer tail added this morning, and a heavy tail holds a kite down
it flew high last Saturday and not today

evidence: “Today he flew it near the school wall.”
“Out in the open field the wind is strong.”
arguments.against: “He added a longer tail this morning.”

evidence: “He added a longer tail this morning.”
“A heavy tail holds a kite down.”
arguments.against: “The wall blocks the wind on that side.”

evidence: “It flew high last Saturday.”
arguments.against: “Out in the open field the wind is strong.”

debate.note: Two things changed since Saturday: where he stood and what he tied on. Ask which one he could change back most easily, and a child will say walk to the field. That is an experiment, and they thought of it themselves.

title: The Case of the Thin Shamrocks
story: Room 9 grew shamrocks in two pots. The plants in one pot are thin and pale. That pot sits far from the window. The other pot sits right on the sill. Plants need light to grow strong. Both pots got the same water. Both pots have the same soil. The thin ones lean toward the window.
question: Why are one pot's shamrocks thin?

suspects.why: that pot sits far from the window
both pots got the same water
both pots have the same soil

answer: The pot far from the window got too little light.
proof: “That pot sits far from the window.”
“Plants need light to grow strong.”
clears: Water: “Both pots got the same water.”
The soil: “Both pots have the same soil.”
explain: The thin ones lean toward the window. Because that pot sits far from the window, those plants did not get enough light.

debate.story: Room 9 grew shamrocks in two pots. The plants in one pot are thin and pale. That pot sits far from the window. The other pot sits right on the sill. Plants need light to grow strong. The far pot also sits above the warm heater. The thin ones lean toward the window.
debate.question: Why are some shamrocks thin? Say which one, and show the words.

suspects.why: a pot far from the window, where plants need light
a pot sitting above the warm heater
thin plants leaning toward the window

evidence: “That pot sits far from the window.”
“Plants need light to grow strong.”
arguments.against: “The far pot also sits above the warm heater.”

evidence: “The far pot also sits above the warm heater.”
arguments.against: “The thin ones lean toward the window.”

evidence: “The thin ones lean toward the window.”
arguments.against: “The other pot sits right on the sill.”

debate.note: Leaning toward the window is a plant telling you what it wants. That is a lovely idea for a seven-year-old and it belongs in the discussion. The heater is a fair answer and it does not explain the lean, which is the gap to point at.

title: The Case of the Wet Floor
story: A wet spot shows up by the door each cold morning. The roof above it does not leak. The sink is far down the hall. Cold glass makes water drops on the inside. The door has a big glass window. The drops run down to the floor. On warm days the floor is dry.
question: Where does the wet spot come from?

suspects.why: the drops run down to the floor
the roof above it does not leak
the sink is far down the hall

answer: Water drops form on the cold glass door.
proof: “Cold glass makes water drops on the inside.”
“The drops run down to the floor.”
clears: A roof leak: “The roof above it does not leak.”
The sink: “The sink is far down the hall.”
explain: On warm days the floor is dry. Because cold glass makes water drops, the door's window drips onto the floor on cold mornings.

debate.story: A wet spot shows up by the door each cold morning. Cold glass makes water drops on the inside. The door has a big glass window. The drops run down to the floor. On warm days the floor is dry. Snow comes in on boots at that same door. The mat by the door was taken away in January.
debate.question: Why is the floor wet? Choose one and read out the words.

suspects.why: cold glass making drops that run down to the floor
snow coming in on boots at that same door

suspects.who: 🧽 The mat that was taken away
suspects.why: a mat taken away in January

evidence: “Cold glass makes water drops on the inside.”
“On warm days the floor is dry.”
arguments.against: “Snow comes in on boots at that same door.”

evidence: “Snow comes in on boots at that same door.”
arguments.against: “The drops run down to the floor.”

evidence: “The mat by the door was taken away in January.”
arguments.against: “The door has a big glass window.”

debate.note: Only on cold mornings is the pattern, and all three suspects happen on cold mornings. That is the point to make. Dry on warm days fits the glass best, because boots and mats do not know what the weather is like until it snows.

title: The Case of the Nibbled Lettuce
story: The garden lettuce has holes in the leaves. The holes are small and round. Slime trails shine on the dirt near the plants. Slugs leave slime when they move. Slugs come out at night. No bird tracks are in the garden. The fence keeps rabbits out. The holes start at the bottom leaves.
question: What is eating the lettuce?

suspects.why: slime trails shine on the dirt
no bird tracks are in the garden
the fence keeps rabbits out

answer: Slugs are eating the lettuce leaves.
proof: “Slime trails shine on the dirt near the plants.”
“Slugs leave slime when they move.”
clears: A bird: “No bird tracks are in the garden.”
A rabbit: “The fence keeps rabbits out.”
explain: The holes start at the bottom leaves and slime trails shine on the dirt. Because slugs leave slime when they move, slugs are eating the lettuce.

debate.story: The garden lettuce has holes in the leaves. The holes are small and round. Slime trails shine on the dirt near the plants. Slugs leave slime when they move. The holes start at the bottom leaves. A bird was seen pecking the bed on Tuesday. The fence has a gap at one corner.
debate.question: What is eating the lettuce? Pick one and show the words.

suspects.why: slime trails on the dirt, and holes starting low
a bird seen pecking the bed on Tuesday
a gap at one corner of the fence

evidence: “Slime trails shine on the dirt near the plants.”
“The holes start at the bottom leaves.”
arguments.against: “A bird was seen pecking the bed on Tuesday.”

evidence: “A bird was seen pecking the bed on Tuesday.”
arguments.against: “Slime trails shine on the dirt near the plants.”

evidence: “The fence has a gap at one corner.”
arguments.against: “The holes are small and round.”

debate.note: Where the holes start is the clue that chooses. Something crawling begins at the bottom and something flying begins at the top. Ask the children to show with their hands where each suspect would eat, and then look at the leaves.

title: The Case of the Quiet Nest
story: Four eggs sat in a nest on the school sign. For two weeks a bird sat on them. This week the nest is empty and clean. No broken shells are on the ground. Tiny tracks lead away in the dust. Baby birds leave the nest when they can fly. The class saw four small birds in the tree.
question: What happened to the eggs?

suspects.why: four small birds are in the tree
no broken shells are on the ground
the class saw four small birds

answer: The eggs hatched and the baby birds flew.
proof: “Baby birds leave the nest when they can fly.”
“The class saw four small birds in the tree.”
clears: A cat: “No broken shells are on the ground.”
Never hatching: “The class saw four small birds in the tree.”
explain: The class saw four small birds in the tree. Because baby birds leave the nest when they can fly, the four eggs hatched.

debate.story: Four eggs sat in a nest on the school sign. For two weeks a bird sat on them. This week the nest is empty and clean. Four small birds now sit in the tree. A cat sits under that sign most days. Baby birds leave the nest when they can fly. One egg was always smaller than the rest.
debate.question: What happened to the eggs? Say which one, and read out the words.

suspects.why: four small birds in the tree, and the nest clean
a cat that sits under that sign most days
one egg that was always smaller than the rest

evidence: “Four small birds now sit in the tree.”
“Baby birds leave the nest when they can fly.”
arguments.against: “A cat sits under that sign most days.”

evidence: “A cat sits under that sign most days.”
arguments.against: “Four small birds now sit in the tree.”

evidence: “One egg was always smaller than the rest.”
arguments.against: “This week the nest is empty and clean.”

debate.note: Four eggs and four birds is counting, and counting is proof a seven-year-old can hold. Ask how many birds there would be if a cat had come. The small egg is there for the children who want to worry about it, and they should be allowed to.

title: The Case of the Litter Corner
story: The school yard is clean but one fence corner is not. Paper collects there every week. The trash can is not broken. No class eats in that corner. The wind blows toward that fence. Paper stops when it hits a fence. Ms. Diaz cleaned it on Monday. It was full again on Friday.
question: Why does paper collect in one corner?

suspects.why: paper stops when it hits a fence
the trash can is not broken
no class eats in that corner

answer: The wind blows paper to that fence.
proof: “The wind blows toward that fence.”
“Paper stops when it hits a fence.”
clears: A broken can: “The trash can is not broken.”
Eating there: “No class eats in that corner.”
explain: It was full again on Friday with nobody eating there. Because the wind blows toward that fence, paper travels across the yard and stops at the corner.

debate.story: The school yard is clean but one fence corner is not. Paper collects there every week. The wind blows toward that fence. Paper stops when it hits a fence. The bus line forms in that same corner at three. The trash can nearest that corner is often full by lunch.
debate.question: Why does paper collect there? Choose one and show the words.

suspects.why: wind blowing toward a fence that stops paper
the bus line forming in that corner at three
a nearest can that is often full by lunch

evidence: “The wind blows toward that fence.”
“Paper stops when it hits a fence.”
arguments.against: “The bus line forms in that same corner at three.”

evidence: “The bus line forms in that same corner at three.”
arguments.against: “Paper stops when it hits a fence.”

evidence: “The trash can nearest that corner is often full by lunch.”
arguments.against: “The school yard is clean but one fence corner is not.”

debate.note: Three different reasons all land in the same corner, which is how real messy corners work. Ask the class for a way to find out: empty the can at lunch for a week, or watch the corner at three, and see which one changes it.

title: The Case of the Blurry Photos
story: The class took photos on the field trip. Many came out blurry. The blurry ones were all taken on the bus. The bus was going fast. The clear ones were taken while standing still. A moving bus shakes the camera. The camera lens was clean. Nobody dropped the camera. The battery was full all day.
question: Why were many photos blurry?

suspects.why: a moving bus shakes the camera
the camera lens was clean
the battery was full all day

answer: The moving bus shook the camera.
proof: “The blurry ones were all taken on the bus.”
“A moving bus shakes the camera.”
clears: A dirty lens: “The camera lens was clean.”
The battery: “The battery was full all day.”
explain: The clear ones were taken while standing still. Because a moving bus shakes the camera, the photos taken on the bus came out blurry.

debate.story: The class took photos on the field trip. Many came out blurry. The blurry ones were all taken on the bus. The bus was going fast. A moving bus shakes the camera. The bus windows were dirty with rain. The clear ones were taken while standing still. The camera went back in its case between stops.
debate.question: Why are the photos blurry? Pick one and read out the words.

suspects.why: all taken on a bus going fast, which shakes the camera
bus windows dirty with rain
the clear ones taken while standing still

evidence: “The bus was going fast.”
“A moving bus shakes the camera.”
arguments.against: “The bus windows were dirty with rain.”

evidence: “The bus windows were dirty with rain.”
arguments.against: “The blurry ones were all taken on the bus.”

evidence: “The clear ones were taken while standing still. The camera went back in its case between stops.”
arguments.against: “A moving bus shakes the camera.”

debate.note: Every blurry photo was taken on the bus, so the bus is certainly part of it. The question is which part. Shaking and a dirty window both happen on a bus, and the class can be asked what a photo through a dirty window would look like.

title: The Case of the Yellow Leaves
story: Two bean plants sit on the class shelf. One has green leaves and one has yellow. The yellow one sits in a pot with no holes. Water fills the bottom of that pot. Roots rot when they sit in water. The green one's pot has three holes. Both plants get the same light.
question: Why are one plant's leaves yellow?

suspects.why: water fills the bottom of that pot
both plants get the same light
the green one's pot has three holes

answer: Water sat in the pot and the roots rotted.
proof: “Water fills the bottom of that pot.”
“Roots rot when they sit in water.”
clears: Light: “Both plants get the same light.”
The other pot: “The green one's pot has three holes.”
explain: The green one's pot has three holes. Because the yellow one's pot has no holes, water sat at the bottom and the roots rotted.

debate.story: Two bean plants sit on the class shelf. One has green leaves and one has yellow. The yellow one sits in a pot with no holes. Water fills the bottom of that pot. Roots rot when they sit in water. The yellow one is further from the window than the green one. It was planted a week later than the green one.
debate.question: Why are the leaves yellow? Say which one, and show the words.

suspects.why: a pot with no holes, with water in the bottom
further from the window than the green one
planted a week later than the green one

evidence: “The yellow one sits in a pot with no holes.”
“Roots rot when they sit in water.”
arguments.against: “The yellow one is further from the window than the green one.”

evidence: “The yellow one is further from the window than the green one.”
arguments.against: “Water fills the bottom of that pot.”

evidence: “It was planted a week later than the green one.”
arguments.against: “One has green leaves and one has yellow.”

debate.note: A week younger would make a plant smaller, not yellow, and that difference is worth drawing out. Yellow is a sick colour, not a young one. Water in the bottom of a pot is something the class can go and check with a finger.

title: The Case of the Soft Ice Cream
story: The class made ice cream in a bag. Six bags turned hard and two stayed soft. The two soft bags had less ice in them. Ice must touch the bag to make it cold. All eight bags got the same shaking. All eight used the same milk. The soft two sat in warm hands.
question: Why did two bags stay soft?

suspects.why: the two soft bags had less ice in them
all eight bags got the same shaking
all eight used the same milk

answer: The two soft bags did not have enough ice.
proof: “The two soft bags had less ice in them.”
“Ice must touch the bag to make it cold.”
clears: Shaking: “All eight bags got the same shaking.”
The milk: “All eight used the same milk.”
explain: All eight bags got the same shaking and the same milk. Because the two soft bags had less ice, the milk never got cold enough.

debate.story: The class made ice cream in a bag. Six bags turned hard and two stayed soft. The two soft bags had less ice in them. Ice must touch the bag to make it cold. The two soft bags were held by the same two children. Those two stopped shaking after one minute. Warm hands on a bag slow the freezing down.
debate.question: Why did two bags stay soft? Choose one and read out the words.

suspects.why: two bags with less ice, and ice must touch to cool
two who stopped shaking after one minute
warm hands on a bag slow the freezing down

evidence: “The two soft bags had less ice in them.”
“Ice must touch the bag to make it cold.”
arguments.against: “Those two stopped shaking after one minute.”

evidence: “Those two stopped shaking after one minute.”
arguments.against: “The two soft bags had less ice in them.”

evidence: “Warm hands on a bag slow the freezing down.”
“The two soft bags were held by the same two children.”
arguments.against: “Ice must touch the bag to make it cold.”

debate.note: The same two bags had less ice, were shaken less and were held by the same hands. Three answers and two bags. Ask what the class would have to do next time to find out, and listen for the child who says give everyone the same ice.

title: The Case of the Torn Ribbon
story: Field day ribbons came in a box. Three had torn tops. The three torn ones hung on the same nail. The nail has a sharp edge. The other ribbons hung on a smooth hook. Nobody pulled on the ribbons. A sharp edge tears cloth. The tears are all in the same spot.
question: What tore the three ribbons?

suspects.why: the three torn ones hung on the same nail
nobody pulled on the ribbons
the other ribbons hung on a smooth hook

answer: The sharp nail tore the three ribbons.
proof: “The three torn ones hung on the same nail.”
“The nail has a sharp edge.”
clears: Pulling: “Nobody pulled on the ribbons.”
The hook: “The other ribbons hung on a smooth hook.”
explain: The tears are all in the same spot. Because the three torn ribbons hung on a nail with a sharp edge, the edge tore the cloth.

debate.story: Field day ribbons came in a box. Three had torn tops. The three torn ones hung on the same nail. The nail has a sharp edge. A sharp edge tears cloth. The three torn ones were also the last three pulled off the nail. The box was carried in under one arm and dropped once.
debate.question: What tore the ribbons? Pick one and show the words.

suspects.why: three on one nail that has a sharp edge
the last three pulled off the nail
a box carried under one arm and dropped once

evidence: “The three torn ones hung on the same nail.”
“The nail has a sharp edge.”
arguments.against: “The three torn ones were also the last three pulled off the nail.”

evidence: “The three torn ones were also the last three pulled off the nail.”
arguments.against: “A sharp edge tears cloth.”

evidence: “The box was carried in under one arm and dropped once.”
arguments.against: “Three had torn tops.”

debate.note: The tears are all at the top, which is where a ribbon hangs and where a hand pulls. A drop would mark anywhere. Ask where each suspect leaves its mark, and let the class check whether all three tears are really in the same place.

title: The Case of the Shrinking Balloons
story: The class blew up balloons on Friday. On Monday they were small and soft. None of them popped. No pins were in the room. Air leaks slowly out of a balloon. The knots are still tied tight. The balloons blown up Monday are still big. Three days passed over the weekend.
question: Why did the balloons get small?

suspects.why: air leaks slowly out of a balloon
no pins were in the room
the knots are still tied tight

answer: Air leaked slowly out of the balloons.
proof: “Air leaks slowly out of a balloon.”
“Three days passed over the weekend.”
clears: A pin: “No pins were in the room.”
Loose knots: “The knots are still tied tight.”
explain: The balloons blown up Monday are still big. Because air leaks slowly out of a balloon, three days made the Friday ones small.

debate.story: The class blew up balloons on Friday. On Monday they were small and soft. Air leaks slowly out of a balloon. Three days passed over the weekend. The balloons blown up Monday are still big. The room was very cold over the weekend. Cold air takes up less room than warm air.
debate.question: Why did the balloons shrink? Say which one, and read out the words.

suspects.why: air leaking slowly, over three days
a very cold room over the weekend
three days passed, and Monday's are still big

evidence: “Air leaks slowly out of a balloon.”
“Three days passed over the weekend.”
arguments.against: “The room was very cold over the weekend.”

evidence: “The room was very cold over the weekend.”
“Cold air takes up less room than warm air.”
arguments.against: “The balloons blown up Monday are still big.”

evidence: “The balloons blown up Monday are still big.”
arguments.against: “Cold air takes up less room than warm air.”

debate.note: If the cold did it, the balloons should get big again now the room is warm. Ask the class to put one on the windowsill and look after lunch. That is a real test and it takes an hour, and the answer is in the room with them.
